Mathematica/Wolfram Language does not have built-in classical OOP in the same way as C# or C++. It is primarily a symbolic, rule-based language. That said, you can still model objects, encapsulate data, and simulate inheritance using associations, symbols, and upvalues.

Common approaches:

1. Use Associations as objects
You can store state in an association:

obj = <|
  "x" -> 3,
  "y" -> 4
|>;

Then define functions that operate on it:

pointX[p_] := p["x"]
pointY[p_] := p["y"]

This is the simplest “object-like” style.

2. Use symbols as mutable objects
A symbol can hold fields in its own definitions.

Clear[PointCreate, PointX, PointY, PointMove]

PointCreate[x_, y_] := Module[{p},
  p = Unique["point"];
  p[x] = x;
  p[y] = y;
  p
]

PointX[p_] := p[x]
PointY[p_] := p[y]

PointMove[p_, dx_, dy_] := (
  p[x] = p[x] + dx;
  p[y] = p[y] + dy;
)

This gives you stateful objects, though it is more “Mathematica-style” than classic OOP.

3. Use patterns and upvalues for methods
A common idiom is to represent an object as a head with data:

ClearAll[Point, Rectangle]

Point /: Coordinates[Point[x_, y_]] := {x, y}
Point /: Move[Point[x_, y_], dx_, dy_] := Point[x + dx, y + dy]

Now:

p = Point[1, 2];
Coordinates[p]
Move[p, 3, 4]

This is a clean functional/OOP hybrid.

4. Simulating inheritance
You can make a “subclass” head that contains a parent object:

Rectangle /: Area[Rectangle[Point[x1_, y1_], Point[x2_, y2_]]] :=
  Abs[(x2 - x1) (y2 - y1)]

Or define shared methods for a more general head structure.

Example:
ClearAll[Point, Rectangle, Move, Coordinates, Area]

Point /: Coordinates[Point[x_, y_]] := {x, y}
Point /: Move[Point[x_, y_], dx_, dy_] := Point[x + dx, y + dy]

Rectangle /: Coordinates[Rectangle[p1_, p2_]] := {Coordinates[p1], Coordinates[p2]}
Rectangle /: Move[Rectangle[p1_, p2_], dx_, dy_] := Rectangle[Move[p1, dx, dy], Move[p2, dx, dy]]
Rectangle /: Area[Rectangle[Point[x1_, y1_], Point[x2_, y2_]]] :=
  Abs[(x2 - x1) (y2 - y1)]

This is not inheritance in the strict OO sense, but it achieves reuse.

5. If you want method dispatch by object type
You can define methods with upvalues on the object head:

obj /: MethodName[obj, args___] := ...

This is often the most idiomatic way to write object-like code in Mathematica.

This difference comes from branch/contour issues in the complex-exponential form, not from the trigonometric identity itself.

The two integrands are algebraically equivalent on the real variable t, but once you rewrite them with exponentials and ask Mathematica to do a symbolic definite integral, it may treat the expression as a complex function and evaluate it via residues. Then the result can depend on which poles are considered inside the contour after analytic continuation.

In short:

- For real t, the two integrands are the same.
- For symbolic a and b, Mathematica may not be able to determine the correct pole configuration in the complex plane.
- The exponential form introduces branch choices and can confuse contour-based evaluation.

Why this happens
-----------------

Using
- cos t = (e^(it) + e^(-it))/2
- sin t = (e^(it) - e^(-it))/(2i)

turns the integrand into a rational function of z = e^(it). That function has poles whose location depends on a and b. For complex parameters, Mathematica has to decide which poles lie inside the unit circle. If it cannot decide, the symbolic result may differ or simplify incorrectly.

A good way to check
-------------------

If you assume a and b are real and positive, the integral has a standard value:

2 pi / (a b)

But if a and b are allowed to be complex, the integral is not uniquely determined without extra assumptions.

What to do
----------

Use assumptions, for example:

Integrate[1/(a^2 Cos[t]^2 + b^2 Sin[t]^2), {t, 0, 2 Pi},
 Assumptions -> Element[{a, b}, Reals] && a > 0 && b > 0]

Or avoid rewriting the integrand into exponentials unless you specifically want complex-contour methods.

So the key point is: the expressions are equivalent on the real line, but not necessarily equivalent in the symbolic complex-analysis machinery Mathematica uses to evaluate them.

This is not really an `ImportString`/`PDF` bug so much as an artifact of how some font outlines are represented.

What you are seeing is an extra zero-length segment at the end of the decoded filled curve:

```wl
Line[{{10.5607, 9.40406}, {10.5607, 9.40406}}]
```

That is just a point drawn as a degenerate line.

Why it happens
- Some fonts/glyphs contain compound outlines or closure markers that produce an extra coordinate pair when imported and decoded.
- `GeometricFunctions`DecodeFilledCurve` preserves that data.
- When you wrap it with `JoinedCurve`, the zero-length segment becomes visible as an extra “dot”.

Why the behavior differs
- Different fonts, platforms, and versions can produce slightly different outline data when exporting to PDF and re-importing.
- So `"Ma"` in default `Style` and `"Ma"` in `Times` may decode differently.
- This is especially common with outline fonts on macOS.

Practical fix
Filter out degenerate lines before using `JoinedCurve`:

```wl
cleanLines = Select[lines, DuplicateFreeQ[First@#] && Length[First@#] > 1 &];
Graphics[JoinedCurve /@ cleanLines]
```

Or more directly, remove zero-length segments:

```wl
cleanLines = DeleteCases[lines, Line[{p_, p_}]];
Graphics[JoinedCurve /@ cleanLines]
```

If you want to be extra safe:

```wl
cleanLines = Select[lines, First[#] =!= Last[#] &];
```

Summary
- The “extra point” is a zero-length line segment in the glyph outline.
- It comes from font/PDF outline encoding, not from `JoinedCurve` itself.
- Filtering out `Line[{p, p}]` cases resolves it.

If you'd like, I can also show how to extract the outlines in a way that avoids `DecodeFilledCurve`/`JoinedCurve` entirely.

```wl
  {x, y, z} /. NSolve[
    Or @@ ({x, y, z} ∈ # & /@ 
        MeshPrimitives[MeshRegion[v1, Line /@ fC], 1]) &&
    Or @@ ({x, y, z} ∈ # & /@ 
        MeshPrimitives[MeshRegion[v2, Polygon /@ f], 2])
```

For example:

```wl

randompoly := Module[{poly},
  While[
    Length[
      FindIntersections[
        poly = PolygonCombine @ SimplePolygonPartition @
          Polygon[RandomReal[{-1, 1}, {25, 2}]]
      ]
    ] > 0
  ];
  poly
]

Graphics[{EdgeForm[Red], Yellow, randompoly}]
```

- `PolygonCombine` merges the parts back
- `FindIntersections` checks whether the result is still self-intersecting
- the `While[...]` loop repeats until a valid simple polygon is found

Use `Fold` on the reversed list, starting from `0`:

```mathematica
continuedFraction[x_List] := Fold[#2/(1 + #) &, 0, Reverse[x]]
```

Example:

```mathematica
continuedFraction[{a, b, c, d}]
```

returns

```mathematica
a/(1 + b/(1 + c/(1 + d)))
```

Why this works:
- `Reverse[x]` processes the list from the end inward.
- `Fold[#2/(1 + #) &, 0, ...]` repeatedly builds the nested fraction.

If you want, I can also show a recursive version.

You can avoid the divergence by stopping the iteration when the remainder becomes 0 and by using a recurrence that works for both irrational and rational inputs.

A clean Mathematica implementation is:

```mathematica
continuedFraction[x_, n_, b_: 1] :=
  Sign[b] Reap[
    NestWhile[
      b/# - Sow@Floor[b/#] &,
      Abs[b]/x,
      # != 0 &,
      1,
      n
    ]
  ][[2, 1]];
```

For negative continued fractions, use `b = -1`:

```mathematica
continuedFraction[Sqrt[2], 10, -1]
```

gives

```mathematica
{2, 2, 4, 2, 4, 2, 4, 2, 4, 2}
```

And for a rational number, it now terminates correctly:

```mathematica
continuedFraction[4/15, 10, -1]
```

returns

```mathematica
{1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2}
```

which corresponds to

```mathematica
1 - 1/(2 - 1/(2 - 1/(3 - 1/(2 - 1/2))))
```

and evaluates back to `4/15`.

This is usually not a Mathematica/Plot bug so much as a font-rendering fallback issue.

What’s happening:
- With `PrivateFontOptions -> {"OperatorSubstitution" -> False}`, the front end is more strict about using the exact glyphs from the chosen font.
- Some fonts, at small point sizes, don’t provide all the glyph metrics/bitmap hints in a way the renderer likes.
- When that happens, the system may silently fall back to another font or render the text inconsistently.
- That’s why you see a threshold size where Ubuntu starts appearing correctly, while other fonts like Inconsolata do not show the problem.

What you can try:
1. Leave operator substitution enabled:
   - `PrivateFontOptions -> {"OperatorSubstitution" -> True}`
   - This is the most robust option for labels and small text.

2. Use a different font family:
   - Some fonts are simply better behaved at small sizes.
   - In your example, Inconsolata works, which supports that this is font-dependent.

3. Increase the font size slightly:
   - If exact appearance matters, bumping the size often avoids the fallback threshold.

4. Test in another output format:
   - For example, export to PDF or PNG and compare.
   - Sometimes the issue is specific to screen rendering rather than the plot itself.

So the short answer is: it’s likely a font/rendering limitation or incompatibility triggered by `OperatorSubstitution -> False`, not a Plot bug per se.

If you mean “how do I make the plot’s displayed size stay the same even when a legend is present?”, the key point is:

ImageSize changes the overall graphic size, not necessarily the internal plot region/frame size.

In Mathematica, legends, labels, and other annotations can change the space reserved around the plot, so two plots with the same PlotRange can still end up with different interior sizes.

What usually works best is one of these:

1. Use the same annotations on both plots
   - Add a dummy legend to the plot without one, so both graphics have the same structure.
   - Then remove or hide the legend contents if needed.
   - This is essentially what the resolved thread does.

2. Explicitly fix the plot region
   - Use options like PlotRegion, ImagePadding, and sometimes PlotRangePadding to control the interior layout.
   - Example:
     Plot[..., ImageSize -> 300, ImagePadding -> {{50, 20}, {20, 20}}]

3. Wrap the finished graphic in a fixed-sized container
   - If you just need consistent output dimensions, use:
     Framed[Show[plot, ImageSize -> 300]]
   - Or set the same ImageSize and ImagePadding for all plots.

Practical recommendation

If you want the size to “stick” across plots with and without legends, set the padding explicitly and keep it identical for all plots, for example:

Plot[
  {f[x], g[x]}, {x, 0, 1},
  PlotRange -> All,
  ImageSize -> 300,
  ImagePadding -> {{50, 20}, {20, 20}}
]

If a legend is involved, give the no-legend plot the same legend layout space, or use the same legend structure in both plots.

- `12.3 -> 12`
- `10.555 -> 10`
- `-12.3 -> -12`

That means it does **not** “round approximate integers”; it just drops the fractional part.

For approximate integers, `Round` is usually the better choice:

```wolfram

```

Example:

```wolfram
Round /@ {123., 56., 45.}
(* {123, 56, 45} *)
```

If you want to leave non-integer reals untouched, you can use a test, e.g.:

```wolfram
If[IntegerQ[Round[#]], Round[#], #] & /@ data
```

or more explicitly:

```wolfram
If[Abs[# - Round[#]] < tol, Round[#], #] & /@ data
```

where `tol` is a small tolerance such as `10^-10`.

So the short answer is:

- **No**, `IntegerPart` is not the most efficient or most appropriate way for approximate integers.
- **Yes**, `Round` is generally the right tool.
- If you need to preserve non-integer reals, add a tolerance-based condition.


For exact integer-valued reals, a more idiomatic approach is:

What Mathematica is doing is not a plain Taylor expansion at the singular point. It is using an asymptotic series expansion that keeps track of logarithmic terms separately.

For your example, near x = 0:

log(x^3 + x^7) = log(x^3(1 + x^4))
= 3 log(x) + log(1 + x^4)

and then

log(1 + x^4) = x^4 + O(x^8).

So Mathematica rewrites the expression into a form that isolates the singular part log(x), and only expands the regular part around 0.

That is why you get something like

(a + 3 log(x))/b + ((-a - 3 log(x)) x)/b^2 + O(x)^2

instead of trying to force a Taylor series in powers of x alone, which would fail because log(x) is singular at 0.

The technique is generally called:
- asymptotic expansion,
- series expansion with logarithmic terms,
- or a transseries-style expansion in some contexts.

So the key point is: this is not an ordinary Taylor series, but an asymptotic series where terms are ordered by size as x -> 0, and log(x) is treated as a separate dominant term.

The issue is that the “expand to the maximum order and then add one O-term per variable” approach does not correctly reproduce a true multivariate Taylor truncation.

Why it fails:
- `Series[expr, {t,0,n}]` only controls the total degree in the dummy variable `t`.
- After substituting `x_i -> t x_i`, every monomial gets weighted by its total degree, so terms can survive even if they exceed the requested order in one variable.
- Adding `O[x_i]^(k+1)` separately does not fully truncate mixed terms consistently.

The accepted approach you included uses a weighting trick:
1. Convert each variable to a weighted power, so that a term’s total degree in a new dummy variable matches the desired multivariate grading.
2. Expand in one dummy variable.
3. Substitute back.

That works well for integer orders.

A cleaned-up version of that idea is:

```mathematica
weightedMultivariateSeries[f_, vars_List, ord_List] /; 
  Length[vars] === Length[ord] && VectorQ[ord, IntegerQ[#] && # > 0 &] :=
 Module[{t, n = Length[ord], lcm = LCM @@ ord, newf},
  newf = f /. Thread[vars -> vars^(lcm/ord)];
  newf = newf /. Thread[vars -> t*vars];
  Normal[Series[newf, {t, 0, Max@(lcm/ord)}]] /. t -> 1 /. 
   Thread[vars -> vars^(ord/lcm)]
 ]
```

Important caveat:
- This version does not handle `Infinity` in `ord`.
- It also assumes positive integers.

If you want to support `Infinity`, a simpler strategy is:
- remove the infinite-order variables from the truncation logic,
- expand only in the finite-order variables,
- then restore the infinite ones unchanged.

Mathematica generally will not solve “two equations for one variable” unless the system is actually consistent and the unknowns are properly specified.

A few common reasons:

1. You may be asking for too few variables  
   If you have 2 equations in 2 unknowns, you should solve for both variables:
   ```mathematica
   Solve[{eq1, eq2}, {x, y}]
   ```

2. The equations may be nonlinear and have no simple closed-form solution  
   In that case, `Solve` may return nothing useful or leave conditions. Try:
   ```mathematica
   Reduce[{eq1, eq2}, {x, y}]
   ```
   or numeric methods if you have numerical values:
   ```mathematica
   NSolve[{eq1, eq2}, {x, y}]
   ```

3. There may be no exact symbolic solution  
   `Solve` is for exact algebraic solutions. If the equations involve transcendental functions, roots, exponentials, logs, etc., `Reduce` or `NSolve` is often better.

4. You might have only one variable in the equations, but two equations  
   Then both equations must be simultaneously satisfied by the same variable. If that is impossible, there is no solution.

If you want to solve the kind of system shown in the thread, the usual form is:

```mathematica
Solve[{f[x, y] == 0, g[x, y] == 0}, {x, y}]
```

If `Solve` fails, try:

```mathematica
Reduce[{f[x, y] == 0, g[x, y] == 0}, {x, y}]
```

and if the equations are numerical:

```mathematica
NSolve[{f[x, y] == 0, g[x, y] == 0}, {x, y}]
```

`Function` has the attribute `HoldAll`, so the body `i*x + j` is not evaluated when `Table` builds the expressions. As a result, `i` and `j` remain symbolic inside each `Function`.

You can verify this with:

```wl
Attributes[Function]
(* {HoldAll, Protected} *)
```

So this:

```wl
Table[Function[x, i*x + j], {i, 1, 3}, {j, 1, 4}]
```

produces unevaluated pure functions containing `i` and `j`.

Ways to force insertion of the loop values:

1. Use `With` to capture the current values:
```wl
Table[
  With[{ii = i, jj = j}, Function[x, ii*x + jj]],
  {i, 1, 3},
  {j, 1, 4}
]
```

2. Use a placeholder and replace it after:
```wl
Table[
  function[x, i*x + j],
  {i, 1, 3},
  {j, 1, 4}
] /. function -> Function
```

3. Or temporarily localize `Function`:
```wl
Block[{Function},
  Table[
    Function[x, i*x + j],
    {i, 1, 3},
    {j, 1, 4}
  ]
]
```

The key point is that `Table` substitutes `i` and `j` into an expression, but `Function` prevents the body from being evaluated until later, so the loop variables never get injected unless you explicitly force that capture.

For example:

g[a___, g[b___], c___] := g[a, b, c]

Then define your commutation rule on the flattened form.

3. Use a wrapper symbol
   Keep one symbol for the algebraic operation and another for storage/normalization.

For example:

expr = G[b, G[G[a, B, c], A]];
expr /. G -> g

Then apply your ordering rule to `g`, not to `G`.

Use rules for the *head* of the function, not for `f[c_]` itself.

In Mathematica/Wolfram Language, derivatives are represented internally as `Derivative[1][f][c]`, so a rule like `f[c_] :> a c` won’t reliably match inside `D[...]`. A better approach is to replace `f` with a pure function.

Example:

```wl
Clear[f, g, a, c]

f$sub = {f :> Function[{c}, a c]};

f[c] //. f$sub
(* a c *)

q (f[c])^2 //. f$sub
(* a^2 c^2 q *)

D[f[c], c] //. f$sub
(* a *)

D[f[c] //. f$sub, c] //. f$sub
(* a *)
```

For your other rules:

```wl
g$sub = {g :> Function[a, a + f[c]]};
g2$sub = {g2 :> Function[a, a + D[f[c], c]]};
```

Then:

```wl
g[a] //. g$sub
(* a + f[c] *)

g[a] //. Union[g$sub, f$sub]
(* a + a c *)
```

Why this works:
- `f[c_] :> ...` matches only explicit calls like `f[c]`.
- `f :> Function[...]` replaces the symbol `f` itself.
- Since `D[f[c], c]` becomes `Derivative[1][f][c]` internally, replacing the head `f` lets the derivative evaluate using the substituted function.

`Print` does not return the value you want to append — it returns `Null`. So if you do something like `AppendTo[list, Print[...]]`, you append `Null`, not the computed vector.

For this task, it’s better to avoid `AppendTo` inside loops. Use `Sow`/`Reap`, or better yet `Table` and `Join`.

### Using `Sow` and `Reap`
```wl
v = {{0, 0, 0}, {1, 0, 0}, {1, 0, 1}, {0, 1, 1}, {1, 1, 1}};

result = Reap[
   For[i = 1, i <= Length[v], i++,
    For[e = 1, e <= Length[v], e++,
     Sow[Mod[v[[i]] + v[[e]], 2]]
    ]
   ]
][[2, 1]];

v = Join[v, result]
```

### Using `Table` instead of loops
```wl
v = {{0, 0, 0}, {1, 0, 0}, {1, 0, 1}, {0, 1, 1}, {1, 1, 1}};

v = Join[v, Flatten[Table[Mod[v[[i]] + v[[e]], 2], {i, 5}, {e, 5}], 1]]
```

### Even cleaner: vectorized form
```wl
v = {{0, 0, 0}, {1, 0, 0}, {1, 0, 1}, {0, 1, 1}, {1, 1, 1}};

v = Join[v, Mod[Plus @@@ Tuples[v, 2], 2]]
```

You generally should not “append” to a list if you want a circular buffer. In Mathematica, the efficient approach is to treat the list as fixed storage and overwrite elements in place, using a moving pointer.

Example:

```mathematica
big = Range@1*^7;
size = Length@big;
pointer = size;

updateElement[new_Integer] := (
  pointer = 1 + Mod[pointer, size];
  big[[pointer]] = new
)
```

Then updates are very fast:

```mathematica
Do[updateElement[RandomInteger@99], {100}] // AbsoluteTiming
```

If you later want the buffer in normal list order, rotate it once:

```mathematica
big = RotateLeft[big, Mod[pointer, size]];
pointer = size;
```

This is much faster than repeatedly doing:

```mathematica
big = Append[Rest@big, new]
```

because that copies the whole list on every step.

Yes — if you want to speed up a series expansion / basis conversion in Mathematica, the key is usually to avoid symbolic “solve the whole system” approaches and instead use orthogonality or recurrence relations.

For Hermite polynomials, the coefficient of the nth term is given by the projection formula:

c_n = <p, H_n> / <H_n, H_n>

with the Hermite inner product

< f, g > = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} f(x) g(x) e^{-x^2} dx.

So instead of expanding by brute force, compute coefficients directly:

```mathematica
p[x_] = 1 + x + x^2 + x^3;

coeffs = Table[
  Integrate[HermiteH[n, x] p[x] Exp[-x^2], {x, -Infinity, Infinity}]/
   Integrate[HermiteH[n, x]^2 Exp[-x^2], {x, -Infinity, Infinity}],
  {n, 0, 3}
]
```

This gives:

```mathematica
{3/2, 5/4, 1/4, 1/8}
```

and reconstructing:

```mathematica
coeffs.Table[HermiteH[n, x], {n, 0, 3}] // Expand
```

returns:

```mathematica
1 + x + x^2 + x^3
```

If your goal is speed, this method is often much faster than generic symbolic basis conversion, especially when the basis is orthogonal.

- how to speed it up further using recurrence relations,
- or how to write a reusable Mathematica function similar to Maple’s `ChangeBasis`.

Yes — the issue is that Mathematica is spending a lot of time trying to decide branch cuts and assumptions for a very nasty algebraic expression near a noninteger power point. It’s not your hardware.

A few things help a lot:

1. Tell Mathematica that `a > 0`
2. Simplify before/after the series
3. If possible, expand around a branch-consistent form instead of the raw expression

For your case, this works much better:

```mathematica
FullSimplify[
  Series[
    (Sqrt[46656 a^2 - 864 (3 2^(1/3) a^(2/3) + 2 a B)^3] + 216 a)^(1/3),
    {a, 0, 2},
    Assumptions -> a > 0
  ]
]
```

This gives a usable series quickly.

Why the slowdown happens:
- The expression contains nested radicals and fractional powers like `a^(2/3)`.
- Near `a = 0`, Mathematica has to infer complex branches.
- Without assumptions, it may try many symbolic paths, which can explode in time.

Also, the kernel becoming sluggish after aborting is a known side effect of interrupting a heavy symbolic computation; restarting the kernel is often the fastest recovery.

If you want, I can also help rewrite the expression into a form that is even faster to series-expand.

In Mathematica, `Series` already computes the coefficients you want, but it returns the whole truncated expansion up to order `t`. To extract only terms from `x^h` through `x^t` without doing two separate series computations, you can work with the internal `SeriesData` representation.

A convenient way is:

```wl
seriespart[f_, {x_, x0_, h_, t_}] := Module[{s, nmin},
  s = Series[f, {x, x0, t}];
  nmin = s[[4]];
  s[[3, (h - nmin + 1) ;; (t - nmin + 1)]] . Table[(x - x0)^i, {i, h, t}]
]
```

Example:

```wl
seriespart[Exp[x], {x, 1, 5, 9}]
```

gives:

```wl
E (-1 + x)^5/120 + E (-1 + x)^6/720 + E (-1 + x)^7/5040 +
E (-1 + x)^8/40320 + E (-1 + x)^9/362880
```

Notes:
- `h` and `t` should be integers with `0 <= h <= t`.
- This avoids computing `Series[f, {x, x0, h - 1}]` separately, so it is usually faster.
- Some series start at powers higher than 0, which is why the `nmin` term is needed.

If you want, I can also show a version that returns a proper `SeriesData` object rather than an expanded polynomial.

`GraphicsGrid` is not really “rescaling” the 3D graphics in the same sense that it is just laying out the cells; the difference is that 3D plots have an aspect-ratio / box-size dependency that 2D plots usually don’t show as strongly.

What’s happening:

- For 2D graphics, `ImageSize -> 200` means “make the graphic 200 pixels wide” and the height is effectively determined by the plot’s aspect ratio or defaults.
- For 3D graphics, `ImageSize` is more naturally interpreted as the overall image dimensions, and if only one number is given, Mathematica may still adjust the final rendered box to preserve the 3D viewpoint and proportions.
- `GraphicsGrid` then tries to fit those rendered boxes into the grid cells, which can make the result look like it’s overriding your `ImageSize`.

So the practical fix is:

```wl
GraphicsGrid@Table[
  Plot3D[Sin[x + y^2], {x, -3, 3}, {y, -2, 2}, ImageSize -> {200, 200}],
  {2}, {2}
]
```

Using `{width, height}` works better for 3D because it gives Mathematica an explicit box size to preserve in the grid.

In short: `ImageSize -> 200` is often sufficient for 2D, but for 3D plots inside `GraphicsGrid`, you usually want `ImageSize -> {w, h}` to prevent the front end from adjusting the display.

Mathematica often has trouble when an equation mixes radicals, trig functions, and inverse trig functions in a nested form. In your example, the issue isn’t that Solve/Reduce can’t do it “if you wait longer” — it’s that the expression is in a form that’s hard for the solver to recognize.

A good trick is to rewrite trig functions in exponential form first, then simplify, and then solve.

For the example from the thread:

```mathematica
Solve[
  FullSimplify[
    TrigToExp[
      -2 (m^2/36 + n^2/4)^(1/4) Sin[1/2 ArcTan[n/2, -(m/6)]] == y
    ]
  ],
  n
]
```

Mathematica returns:

```mathematica
{{n -> (m^2 - 9 y^4)/(18 y^2)}}
```

So the reason it “won’t solve” directly is usually one of these:

- the equation is too algebraically complex in its current form
- inverse trig functions create branch-cut/complexity issues
- `Solve` works best after you transform the expression into a simpler equivalent form

This is usually caused by the button action running in the front end’s immediate evaluation path and then blocking on `Input[...]`, which can make the Dynamic/FE interaction hang.

Use a queued button action instead:

```wl

 Dynamic @ Panel @
  Row@{
    Button["Built In Funct", openNothing[], Method -> "Queued"]
  },
 Initialization :> (openNothing[] := (Input["bla", 1];))
]
```

Why this helps:
- `Method -> "Queued"` sends the button action to the kernel queue instead of evaluating it immediately in the front end.

What you’re seeing is the same preemptive-vs-queued evaluation issue.

A `Button` action is not guaranteed to stay in the front-end event loop long enough for your side effects to happen in the order you expect. If the action includes something like `Pause`, the evaluation can get interrupted / preempted before the later parts finish, even if the output cells already exist.

So yes: even if the `Dynamic` cells for `x` and `y` are already there, you still need

```wl

```

if you want the whole action to run sequentially and reliably.

Why your expectation fails:
- `Button` actions default to preemptive evaluation.
- Preemptive evaluation can yield control back to the front end.
- `Pause` is especially sensitive to this, because it explicitly suspends evaluation.
- So the code after `Pause` may not run when you think it will.

For a custom button based on `EventHandler`, the same warning applies. If you use something like:

```wl
SetAttributes[GButton, HoldRest]
GButton[ob_, proc_] := DynamicModule[{},
  EventHandler[
    Framed[ob, Alignment -> Center],
    {"MouseDown" :> (proc)},
    PassEventsUp -> False,
    PassEventsDown -> False
  ]
]
```

then `proc` is still being triggered from the front end event system, and if `proc` contains delayed side effects or `Pause`, you can run into the same kind of timing problem.

The safe rule:
- If you need “click -> do this, then wait, then do that” behavior, use queued evaluation.
- If you build your own click handler with `EventHandler`, you may need to wrap the action so it is effectively queued or otherwise delayed into a `Dynamic`/`Refresh`-driven mechanism.

The workaround shown in the resolved thread is basically:
- use a trigger variable,
- let the mouse event only set that trigger,
- then let a `Dynamic`/`Refresh` do the actual work.

That avoids relying on the event handler itself to execute the whole computation synchronously.

In short: yes, you do still need `Method -> "Queued"` for that case, and with `EventHandler`-based buttons you should assume the same preemptive-evaluation caveat unless you explicitly move the computation into a queued/dynamic mechanism.

A `Button` action is evaluated differently from a plain input line.

`Button["X", Print@1; Pause@1; Print@2]` runs on a preemptive evaluation link. That means the front end interrupts normal queued evaluation so the button can respond quickly, but the action is only allowed a limited amount of time to run. Because of that, the action may not complete the full sequence before the front end moves on, so the behavior can look different from just typing:

`Print@1; Pause@1; Print@2`

If you want the button to behave like normal sequential evaluation, use:

`Button["X", Print@1; Pause@1; Print@2, Method -> "Queued"]`

`Method -> "Queued"` runs the action in the regular evaluation queue, so `Print[1]`, then the pause, then `Print[2]` happen in order without the preemptive time limit.

In short:

- default button action: preemptive, time-limited
- `Method -> "Queued"`: normal queued evaluation, same as entering the code directly

If you want, I can also explain the difference between preemptive, queued, and synchronous dynamics in Wolfram Language.

Yes — if you use `EventHandler` directly, the handler code is still subject to the notebook’s normal dynamic/preemptive evaluation behavior unless you explicitly force a queued evaluation or otherwise defer the work.

### Why your `Pause` appears to run “first”
In your example, the click event is being handled in a context where the front end may start evaluating the action preemptively. That means:

- the event is noticed immediately,
- the handler expression is queued/preempted according to the surrounding evaluation rules,
- `Pause` does **not** guarantee that later UI updates or newly created cells have time to appear first.

So even though visually it feels like “the button was clicked, then the cells should already exist,” the actual kernel evaluation order is not necessarily what you expect.

### For `Button`
Using:

```wl
Button["X", x = 3; Pause[1]; y = 4, Method -> "Queued"]
```

forces the button action to run in the kernel’s queued evaluation stream, which is why it behaves more predictably.

### For a custom `EventHandler` button
Your custom version:

```wl
SetAttributes[GButton, HoldRest]
GButton[ob_, proc_] := DynamicModule[{},
  EventHandler[
    Framed[ob, Alignment -> Center],
    {"MouseDown" :> (proc)},
    PassEventsUp -> False,
    PassEventsDown -> False
  ]
]
```

does **not** automatically replicate `Button[..., Method -> "Queued"]`. So if `proc` contains delayed or interactive work, you may still see preemptive behavior.

### Practical workaround
If you want event-driven behavior that waits until the click is fully processed, wrap the action so it is triggered by a dynamic/queued mechanism rather than executed directly inside the event handler.

A common workaround is the pattern from the resolved thread:

```wl
DynamicModule[{trigger = 0},
 DynamicWrapper[
  EventHandler[
   Framed["Benjamin Button"],
   "MouseDown" :> (++trigger)
  ],
  If[trigger =!= 0,
   Refresh[
    Pause[3];
    Print["If you couldn't, it was preemptive"],
    None
   ]
  ],
  SynchronousUpdating -> False
 ]
]
```

### Key point
- `Button[..., Method -> "Queued"]` is the clean solution for `Button`.
- A custom `EventHandler`-based button does **not** inherit that behavior automatically.
- If you need guaranteed ordering, you must build that queueing/deferred evaluation behavior yourself.

### Bottom line
So the answer to “why doesn’t it work the way I thought?” is: because the handler is still being evaluated in the notebook’s dynamic/preemptive framework, and `Pause` does not force the front end to wait for UI changes or cell creation. If the order matters, use queued evaluation explicitly.

If you want, I can show a cleaner `GButton` implementation that behaves more like `Button[..., Method -> "Queued"]`.

What’s going wrong is that `Button`’s action is being evaluated in a way that blocks the front end while `InputString` waits for input.

`InputString` is a synchronous, modal kernel-side prompt. When you put it directly inside a `Button`, the click starts the button action, but then the kernel is held waiting for the string, and the front end can become unresponsive because it’s already tied up handling that interaction. That’s why you see the spinning cursor and end up needing to abort.

In short:

- `Button` is not a good place for a blocking input function like `InputString`
- the front end and kernel get stuck waiting on each other
- this is effectively a usability bug / design limitation in that version

How to do it instead:

1. Use `InputField` or `Manipulate`
   - Best if you want a user-editable value in the notebook itself.

2. Use a dialog function designed for GUI interaction
   - `DialogInput` / `CreateDialog` are the usual tools.

Example:

```wl
Button["Ask for input",
  DialogInput[
    str = InputField[Dynamic[val], String];
    Column[{
      str,
      DefaultButton[DialogReturn[val]]
    }]
  ]
]
```

Or simpler, if you just want a prompt:

```wl
Button["Ask",
  DialogInput[
    val = Input["Type something"]
  ]
]
```

But in general, for button-driven interactions, prefer GUI elements (`InputField`, `DialogInput`, `CreateDialog`, `DynamicModule`) over `InputString`.

In Mathematica/Wolfram Language, a `Module` does not give you a “private context” in the OO sense. It only creates unique local symbols like `balance$12345`. Those symbols still live in the global symbol table, but their generated names prevent collisions.

So the usual way to make module-local state “belong” to an object is to capture it inside a unique symbol or inside closures/UpValues.

A good pattern is:

1. Create an object representation with `Module`
2. Keep state in local symbols
3. Expose behavior through functions or UpValues tied to that object

Example using an object-like wrapper:

```wl
SetAttributes[account, HoldAll];

makeAccount[initBalance_] :=
 Module[{balance = initBalance},
  account[balance]
 ]

account /: balance[account[bal_]] := bal
account /: deposit[account[bal_], amount_] := (bal += amount)
account /: withdraw[account[bal_], amount_] := If[amount <= bal, bal -= amount, "Insufficient funds"]
```

Usage:

```wl
a1 = makeAccount[100];
a2 = makeAccount[150];

balance[a1]
deposit[a1, 100]
balance[a1]
balance[a2]
```

Why this works:
- `balance` inside `Module` becomes a unique symbol
- `account[...]` stores that unique symbol’s value
- UpValues define behavior specific to that object

If you want no `SetAttributes`, you can instead return a closure:

```wl
makeAccount1[initBalance_] :=
 Module[{balance = initBalance},
  Function[msg,
   Switch[msg,
    "balance", balance,
    "deposit", Function[amount, balance += amount],
    "withdraw", Function[amount, If[amount <= balance, balance -= amount, "Insufficient funds"]],
    _, "Unknown request"
   ]
  ]
 ]
```

This is often the most robust way to give each “module” its own state in Wolfram Language.

- how to keep several private methods and variables,
- or how `Module`, `Block`, and `With` differ for scoping.

- Attach a custom `CellEvaluationFunction`
- Have that function send the cell contents to the system shell
- Optionally replace the input cell after evaluation so it behaves more like a terminal prompt

Example helper from the answer:

```mathematica
evaluatableCell[label_String, evaluationFunction_] :=
  ( CellPrint[
      TextCell[
        ""
      , "Program"
      , Evaluatable -> True
      , CellEvaluationFunction -> evaluationFunction
      , CellFrameLabels -> {{None, label}, {None, None}}
      , CellGroupingRules -> "InputGrouping"
      ]

  ; SelectionMove[EvaluationNotebook[], All, EvaluationCell]
  ; NotebookDelete[]
  ; SelectionMove[EvaluationNotebook[], Next, CellContents]
```

```mathematica
evaluatableCell["shell", Import["!" ~~ #, "Text"] &]
```

- This setup deletes the original input after evaluation and creates a fresh cell, which makes it feel terminal-like.

Because the two expressions are mathematically equal, but a CAS or symbolic package may not automatically rewrite them the way you expect.

Mathematically:

\[
\iint (x^2+y^2)f(x,y)\,dx\,dy
=
\iint x^2 f(x,y)\,dx\,dy+\iint y^2 f(x,y)\,dx\,dy
\]

by linearity of the integral.

Why a system may not show that form automatically:
- It may keep the integral unevaluated and treat the whole integrand as one object.
- It may only distribute multiplication over addition at the algebraic level, but not rewrite an integral into a sum unless explicitly told to.
- In some systems, the integral operator is not automatically expanded because doing so can change how later rules match.

If you want to force the expansion, you usually need to apply a rule like “distribute the integral over sums” or explicitly rewrite the integrand first.

In generic symbolic terms, the transformation is:

\[
\int (u+v)\,dx \to \int u\,dx + \int v\,dx
\]

and more generally:

\[
\int \sum_i u_i\,dx \to \sum_i \int u_i\,dx
\]

So if your goal is to later match
\[
\iint x^2 f(x,y)\,dx\,dy \to a
\]
then you need the expression rewritten into a sum of separate integrals first, either by:
- expanding the integrand before integration, or
- applying a linearity/distribution rule to the integral.

They aren’t equal because this is a Mathematica bug in symbolic integration, not a mathematical discrepancy.

What’s happening is that Mathematica is handling the nested integration order poorly for your original `limits`:

```mathematica
{ux, 0, L}, {vx, 0, L}, {uy, 0, ux}, {vy, 0, vx}
```

This “hanging” dependency between variables seems to confuse `Integrate` when the expressions are reused and combined in different ways. So the two mathematically equivalent computations:

- integrating the linear combination directly, and
- integrating each term separately and then combining

produce inconsistent results.

The workaround is to change the order of integration so the dependent variables come immediately after the variables they depend on:

```mathematica
limits = Sequence[{ux, 0, L}, {uy, 0, ux}, {vx, 0, L}, {vy, 0, vx}];
```

With that order, both methods agree and give:

```mathematica
(1 - E^(-L^2 ρ)) L^2
```

So the short answer is: the additions of integrals and summations *should* be equal, but Mathematica’s symbolic engine is making an error for that integration order. Changing the order of limits fixes it.

Because both addition and summation/integration are only guaranteed to be linear under certain conditions, and Mathematica is being conservative about when it applies that rule.

In the thread you quoted, the key point is:

- `Integrate` does not always automatically split a sum if some parts are not integrable.
- `Distribute` can be used to force linearity over `Plus` before integration.

Example from the answer:

```mathematica
Integrate[integrand, mp] // Distribute
```

This works by distributing the integral over the sum, giving separate terms:
- the polynomial parts are integrated
- the hard part stays as an unevaluated integral

Why the additions aren’t “equal” in the way you expect:
- `Integrate[a + b, x]` is not always transformed into `Integrate[a, x] + Integrate[b, x]` automatically, because that can change what Mathematica returns when only part of the expression is integrable.
- Likewise, `Sum` and `Integrate` are linear mathematically, but symbolic systems may avoid using that property unless explicitly told to.

So if you want the linearity to be applied term-by-term, use something like:

```mathematica
Distribute[Integrate[integrand, mp]]
```

or manually expand/split the sum first.

If you want, I can also explain the difference between `Distribute`, `Expand`, and `Linearize`-style rewrites in Mathematica.

`Assumptions` only works with actual assumptions, i.e. equations or inequalities, not replacement rules.

So instead of giving something like rules, use conditions such as:

```mathematica
Assumptions -> {a > 0, b > 0, x ∈ Reals}
```

or, if you want parameter relations, use equations/inequalities like:

```mathematica
Assumptions -> {m == n, c > 0}
```

A few important points:

- `Integrate` does not always fully exploit assumptions.
- Often the right approach is:
  1. compute the integral,
  2. then simplify the result with `FullSimplify` using your assumptions.

Example pattern:

```mathematica
FullSimplify[
  Integrate[f[x], x],
  Assumptions -> {a > 0, b > 0}
]
```

If you currently have replacement rules, convert them into logical conditions before using them in `Assumptions`.

`Sum` is evaluating the summand symbolically, not by “trying out” the integer values one by one.

In your original input:

```mathematica
Sum[Boole[!IntegerQ[x]], {x, 1, Infinity}]
```

`x` is treated as an integer summation variable, but `IntegerQ[x]` is not automatically simplified to `True` under that assumption, so `Sum` cannot prove the terms are all zero and issues `Sum::div`.

Why the workaround works
------------------------

This version:

```mathematica
Sum[Boole[!(IntegerPart[x] == x)], {x, 1, Infinity}]
```

does simplify for integer `x`, because `IntegerPart[x] == x` is something Mathematica can reduce when `x` is known to be an integer. So the summand becomes `0`, and the sum evaluates to:

```mathematica
0
```

Why your function definition didn’t help
----------------------------------------

You wrote:

```mathematica
intq[x_?NumericQ] := IntegerQ[x];
Sum[Boole[! intq[x]], {x, 1, Infinity}]
```

But `intq[x]` only applies when `x` matches `NumericQ`. In the symbolic preprocessing that `Sum` does, it may not evaluate the way you expect, so the expression stays unevaluated.

What to do instead
------------------

Use an expression that simplifies under integer assumptions, for example:

```mathematica
Sum[Boole[! (IntegerPart[x] == x)], {x, 1, Infinity}]
```

or explicitly tell Mathematica that `x` is an integer:

```mathematica
Simplify[Boole[!IntegerQ[x]], Element[x, Integers]]
```

which gives `0`.

If you want, I can also explain why `IntegerQ[x]` is not enough for `Sum` even though `x` is the summation index.

Use a slice of the list instead of the full dataset.

For example, if you only want the first 100 rows:

```wolfram

Show[
  BarChart[data[[;; 100]], ChartLegends -> {"TX", "RX"}],
  ImageSize -> 600
]
```

If you want a different range, use part extraction:

- `data[[1 ;; 100]]` → rows 1 through 100
- `data[[0 ;; 100]]` is not valid in Wolfram Language indexing
- `data[[50 ;; 150]]` → rows 50 through 150

So the key is to plot only the portion of `data` you want, e.g. `data[[;;100]]`.

Why this happens:

So the fix is to increase `PlotPoints` (and optionally `MaxRecursion`) for finer detection.

If you have a list of sampled points `{x_i, y_i}`, the trapezoidal rule is easy to implement directly.

For points stored as a list like:

```mathematica
t = Table[{x, Sin[x]}, {x, 0, Pi, .01}];
```

you can compute the integral as:

```mathematica
1/2 Total[((#[[2, 1]] - #[[1, 1]]) (#[[2, 2]] + #[[1, 2]])) & /@ Partition[t, 2, 1]]
```

This gives approximately:

```mathematica
1.99998
```

A shorter equivalent version is:

```mathematica
1/2 Total[Differences[t[[All, 1]]] ListCorrelate[{1, 1}, t[[All, 2]]]]
```

This is just the trapezoidal formula:

\[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx \approx \frac12 \sum_{k=1}^N (x_{k+1}-x_k)\,(f(x_{k+1})+f(x_k))
\]

If you already have separate `x` and `y` lists, you can write it as:

```mathematica
1/2 Total[Differences[x] (Most[y] + Rest[y])]
```

That’s often the simplest form.

For a minimal-effort C++ integration strategy in Mathematica, the key idea is: avoid `expr[[...]]` directly on something that may stay symbolic during solver evaluation. Use a function interface that takes the desired component as an argument, so the part selection happens only after the numeric function has been called.

A clean pattern is:

```mathematica
ClearAll[f]

f[y_?NumericQ, part_: All] := {NIntegrate[z*y, {z, 0, 1}], a y}[[part]]
```

Then in `NDSolve`:

```mathematica
NDSolve[{y'[t] == f[y[t], 1], y[0] == 1}, y[t], {t, 0, 5}]
```

If you want the full list by default:

```mathematica
f[3.6]
(* {1.8, 3.6 a} *)
```

Another equivalent approach is to make the part extraction its own function:

```mathematica
ClearAll[f, listPart]

listPart[x_List, part__] := x[[part]]

f[y_?NumericQ] := {NIntegrate[z*y, {z, 0, 1}], a y}

NDSolve[{y'[t] == f[y[t]] ~listPart~ 1, y[0] == 1}, y[t], {t, 0, 5}]
```

If your real goal is integrating C++ functions into Mathematica, the same principle applies: expose a numeric function that returns either a scalar or a list, and select components through an explicit argument rather than by applying `[[...]]` directly in the solver equation.

If you want, I can also show the most direct way to wrap a C++ function via LibraryLink or MathLink/WSTP in this style.

You generally do not want to pass those constraint expressions directly as a `RealList` to C++.

What you have in Mathematica is a list of symbolic inequalities, not just numeric data. So your C++ side would need either:

1. a symbolic parser/handler via MathLink/WSTP, or
2. a preprocessing step in Mathematica that converts the constraints into plain numeric arrays before sending them to C++.

For this problem, the simplest approach is usually option 2.

## If you only need the coefficients
Your constraints are all of the form:

- quadratic circle-like constraints
- linear inequalities

For example:

```mathematica
-1 + (-0.363263 + x)^2 + (-0.329466 + y)^2 <= 0
```

can be expanded in Mathematica and rewritten into coefficients. You can extract the constants and build matrices/vectors in Mathematica, then send only those to C++.

Example idea:

```mathematica
constraints = {
  -1 + (-0.363263 + x)^2 + (-0.329466 + y)^2 <= 0,
  -1 + (-0.248721 + x)^2 + (0.451803 + y)^2 <= 0
  (* etc. *)
};
```

Then use Mathematica to manipulate them into a standardized form like:

```mathematica
a x^2 + b y^2 + c x + d y + e <= 0
```

and export `{a,b,c,d,e}` for each constraint.

## If you want to stay in Mathematica
The resolved thread you provided suggests something important: in this specific case, using Mathematica’s built-in optimizers may already be fast enough.

For the posted constraints, the objective is just `t`, and the problem is very small. The answer shows:

```mathematica
NMinimize[{t, quadraticcons && linearcons}, {x, y, t}]
FindMinimum[{t, quadraticcons && linearcons}, {x, y, t}]
```

and notes that `FindMinimum` is quite fast here.

So before building a MathLink/WSTP interface, it would be worth trying the built-in solvers first.

## If you still want C++
Then your C++ function signature should probably not be something like `RealList` for the raw constraints. Instead, use one of these:

- a list of symbolic expressions received through WSTP, then parse them in C++
- a numeric parameter list, after Mathematica preprocesses the expressions

The second option is much easier.

## Recommendation
Best practical workflow:

1. In Mathematica, transform each constraint into coefficient form.
2. Send only numbers to C++.
3. Let C++ solve the optimization.
4. Return the result to Mathematica.

If you want, I can show you how to write a Mathematica function that converts your exact constraint list into coefficient matrices for C++ ingestion.

The minimal-effort answer is: use C++ if you want a real standalone application with timers, threading, low-level input handling, and a polished GUI.

If your goal is to *reuse some C++ code inside Mathematica*, that is possible, but it is usually not the easiest path for building the whole app.

Practical options:

1. Best for a real desktop app: C++ + Qt
- Native standalone executable
- Good GUI controls
- Easy timers, threads, mouse/keyboard events
- Much better for distribution and maintainability

2. If you want Mathematica as the front end:

- This is the standard way to integrate external C/C++ code

3. If you want “Mathematica-only” GUI apps:
- Possible for prototypes, demos, or internal tools
- Not ideal for serious standalone deliverables
- Distribution is awkward, and many GUI capabilities are limited compared with Qt/C++

So, for “minimal effort method for integrating C++ functions into Mathematica,” the usual recommendation is:

- Write the performance/algorithm code in C++
- Expose it through WSTP/MathLink
- Call it from Mathematica

But if your real goal is a full standalone GUI program, then the simplest and safest choice is to stay in C++ with Qt.

In short:
- Need standalone app? C++/Qt
- Need Mathematica for computation and C++ for speed? Mathematica + WSTP/MathLink
- Need easy delivery and GUI polish? Avoid Mathematica as the main app framework

Mathematica does not have a built-in “suspend/resume after reboot” feature like a VM snapshot.

What you can do instead is make your computation restartable by saving its state periodically, then loading that state when you relaunch Mathematica.

Typical approaches:

1. Save intermediate results to a file
- Use Save, DumpSave, Export, or Put during the computation.
- On startup, read the file back and continue.

Example:
```mathematica
If[FileExistsQ["state.mx"],
  Get["state.mx"],
  state = <|"step" -> 0, "data" -> {}|>
]

Do[
  (* work *)
  state["step"] = i;
  AppendTo[state["data"], result];

  If[Mod[i, 10] == 0, DumpSave["state.mx", state]],
  {i, state["step"] + 1, 1000}
]
```

2. Write your computation as a loop with checkpoints
- Periodically store progress markers, partial outputs, or key variables.
- After a restart, resume from the last checkpoint.

3. Use a notebook or package file for persistent definitions
- If the issue is just avoiding loss of code, save the notebook/package to disk.
- But note: this does not preserve the live kernel state across reboot.

4. Consider Abort-safe / resume-friendly design
- Break long work into smaller units.
- Avoid relying on fragile in-memory-only state.

If you want something closer to true suspend/resume, that is generally handled by the operating system or a virtual machine, not by Mathematica itself.

The error means J/Link cannot load the native DLL, not that the remote kernel connection itself is wrong.

Most likely causes:

1. Wrong DLL architecture
   - If your Java is 64-bit, you need the 64-bit JLinkNativeLibrary.dll.
   - If your Java is 32-bit, you need the 32-bit DLL.
   - The DLLs are in different folders in the J/Link distribution:
     - 32-bit: JLink/SystemFiles/Libraries/Windows/
     - 64-bit: JLink/SystemFiles/Libraries/Windows-x86-64/

2. J/Link is not arranged in its normal folder layout
   - J/Link is designed to find its native library automatically when JLink.jar stays with the rest of the J/Link files from the Mathematica installation.
   - If you copied only JLink.jar or only the DLL to “My Documents”, J/Link may not be able to locate it.

Recommended fix:
- Put the full J/Link directory structure in place, or better:
- Add the original JLink.jar from the Mathematica installation to your Java classpath and do not move the DLL out of the J/Link tree.

Example:
- Keep something like this intact:
  mydir/
    JLink.jar
    SystemFiles/
      Libraries/
        Windows-x86-64/
          JLinkNativeLibrary.dll

If you want to use a custom location, your property approach is valid:
- `com.wolfram.jlink.libdir` should point to the exact folder containing the correct DLL.

So check:
- the path is correct,
- the DLL matches your Java bitness,
- and preferably use the J/Link files from the original Mathematica layout instead of copying them separately.

If you want, I can also show you how to verify whether your Java is 32-bit or 64-bit.

A common cause of `MLECONNECT` when launching a remote Mathematica kernel through J/Link is that the kernel starts, but the front end can’t complete the link handshake. The resolved setup that worked here was:

1. Use password-less SSH between the local machine and the remote host.
   - Generate an SSH key pair on your local machine.
   - Copy the public key to the remote machine’s `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`.

2. Put `init.m` on the remote machine:
   - Copy `init.m` into:
     `~/.Mathematica/Kernel/`

3. Put `tunnel.sh` on the local machine:
   - Copy `tunnel.sh` into:
     `~/Library/Mathematica/FrontEnd/`

4. In Mathematica, add a remote kernel via:
   - `Evaluation -> Kernel Configuration Options -> Add`
   - Choose `Advanced Options`

5. Set **Arguments for MLOpen** to:
   - `-LinkMode Listen -LinkProtocol TCPIP -LinkOptions MLDontInteract -LinkHost 127.0.0.1`

6. Set **Arguments for Launch command** to something like:
   - `"/Users/Account/Library/Mathematica/FrontEnd/tunnel.sh" user@remote.machine:port "wolfram" "`linkname`"`

   Replace:
   - `Account` with your macOS username
   - `user` with the remote login name
   - `remote.machine` with the remote host/IP
   - `port` with the remote SSH port

7. Make sure `wolfram` is available on the remote machine’s PATH.

Notes:
- This was tested with Mathematica 11.2 on macOS client and Linux server.
- It may take some time to establish the connection.
- You can check the log file in:
  `~/Library/Mathematica/FrontEnd/`

Use `FullSimplify`, not just `Simplify`.

For example:

```mathematica
z = Exp[2 Pi I/5];
Z = {{z, 1}, {0, 1/z}};
FullSimplify[MatrixPower[Z, 5]] // MatrixForm
```

This gives the identity matrix.

Why `Simplify` fails here: Mathematica doesn’t always automatically recognize that those fifth roots of unity sum to zero in the algebraic form it produces.

If you want a more targeted and sometimes faster approach, you can convert powers like `(-1)^(1/5)` into trig form first:

```mathematica
ExpToTrig[MatrixPower[Z, 5]]
```

That rewrites the roots as `Cos[...] + I Sin[...]`, and then the cancellation becomes obvious.

So the short answer is:

- use `FullSimplify` for the general solution
- use `ExpToTrig` if you specifically want to expose roots of unity in trig form

`Plot` has the attribute `HoldAll`, so it does not evaluate its first argument before setting up the plot.

That means in

```mathematica
Plot[Fit[med, {1, x}, x], {x, 0, 10}]
```

the `Fit[...]` expression is held unevaluated when `Plot` starts working, so `Plot` cannot immediately turn it into a numeric function of `x`.

Using

```mathematica
Plot[Evaluate @ Fit[med, {1, x}, x], {x, 0, 10}]
```

forces `Fit[...]` to be computed first, producing an explicit polynomial/expression in `x`, and then `Plot` can sample it.

You can verify the reason with:

```mathematica
Attributes[Plot]
```

which returns:

```mathematica
{HoldAll, Protected}
```

So the rule of thumb is:

- if the function can be evaluated before plotting, wrap it in `Evaluate`
- especially when the expression is constructed by functions like `Fit`, `Solve`, `DSolve`, etc.

Example:

```mathematica
f = Fit[med, {1, x}, x];
Plot[f, {x, 0, 10}]
```

or directly:

```mathematica
Plot[Evaluate @ Fit[med, {1, x}, x], {x, 0, 10}]
```

In Mathematica, once you have a fit object, you plot it like any other function.

For example, if you did something like:

```wl
fit = Fit[data, {1, x, x^2}, x]
```

then you can plot the fitted curve with:

```wl
Plot[fit, {x, xmin, xmax}]
```

or overlay it on your data:

```wl
Show[
  ListPlot[data, PlotStyle -> Red],
  Plot[fit, {x, xmin, xmax}, PlotStyle -> Blue]
]
```

A more common workflow is:

```wl
data = {{0., -0.2203}, {0.034, -0.2075}, (* etc. *)};

fit = Fit[data, {1, x, x^2, x^3}, x];

Show[
  ListPlot[data, PlotStyle -> Red, PlotMarkers -> Automatic],
  Plot[fit, {x, Min[data[[All, 1]]], Max[data[[All, 1]]]},
    PlotStyle -> Blue]
]
```

If you used `FindFit`, it returns parameter rules, so you first build the fitted function:

```wl
params = FindFit[data, a + b x + c x^2, {a, b, c}, x];
f[x_] = a + b x + c x^2 /. params;

Plot[f[x], {x, 0, 2}]
```

Then overlay with:

```wl

  Plot[f[x], {x, 0, 2}]
```

In `Plot`, `Exclusions` is mainly for telling Mathematica where the plotted expression is discontinuous or not well-defined, so it can break the curve there. It works best when you give it a condition that is directly about the variable being plotted.

For your rational function

```mathematica
h[x_] := ((x - 3) (x - 4))/((x - 2) (x - 5))
```

the vertical asymptotes are where the denominator is zero, so these are the right exclusions:

```mathematica
Plot[h[x], {x, 0, 7},
  Exclusions -> {x == 2, x == 5},
  ExclusionsStyle -> Dashed]
```

or equivalently:

```mathematica
Plot[h[x], {x, 0, 7},
  Exclusions -> { (x - 2) (x - 5) == 0 },
  ExclusionsStyle -> Dashed]
```

Using

```mathematica
Exclusions -> {h[x] == 0}
```

does not mean “exclude the asymptotes.” It means “exclude where the function is zero,” which is the opposite of what you want. Zeros of the function are not singularities.

Why `Tan[x]` works:
`Tan[x]` has asymptotes where `Cos[x] == 0`, so this is a direct way to specify the discontinuities:

```mathematica
Plot[Tan[x], {x, 0, 4 Pi},
  Exclusions -> {Cos[x] == 0},
  ExclusionsStyle -> Directive[Gray, Dashed]]
```

For a general function from the book, the same idea applies: exclude where the denominator is zero, or where the function is undefined/discontinuous. If you only know the function itself and not its denominator, you may need to derive those points first.

If you want Mathematica to find discontinuities automatically, you can also try:

```mathematica
Plot[h[x], {x, 0, 7}, Exclusions -> Automatic]
```

But for symbolic functions like rational expressions, it’s usually better to specify the exclusions yourself.

So the key point is:

- `f[x] == 0` excludes roots
- denominator `== 0` excludes vertical asymptotes

If you want, I can also show how to make Mathematica automatically detect the asymptotes of a rational function.

Yes. In Mathematica, the usual way to draw different parts of different curves in one `Plot` is to either:

1. use `ConditionalExpression` for the individual expressions, or
2. use `RegionFunction` to restrict where each curve is drawn.

For your case, the cleanest approach is often to put everything into one `Plot` and condition the two dashed curves so they stop at the intersection point.

Example:

```wl
Manipulate[
 Rotate[
  Plot[
   {
    ConditionalExpression[a (\[Eta] - 1)^2, 0 < \[Eta] <= 1],
    ConditionalExpression[a (\[Eta] + 1)^2, -1 < \[Eta] <= 0],
    xL + 0.2*\[Theta][2][\[Eta], \[Xi], Nterms],
    xL
   },
   {\[Eta], -1, 1},
   PlotRange -> {{-1, 1}, {0, 1}},
   Filling -> {3 -> xL},
   PlotStyle -> {
     Directive[Thick, Dashed, ColorData[1, 2]],
     Directive[Thick, Dashed, ColorData[1, 2]],
     Directive[Thick, ColorData[1, 1]],
     Directive[Thick, ColorData[1, 2]]
   },
   AspectRatio -> 1.5
  ],
  rotateAngle
 ],
 {\[Xi], 0, 0.1},
 {xL, 0, 1},
 {{a, 1}, 0, 1},
 {{rotateAngle, -Pi/2}, {0, -Pi/2}}
]
```

This makes the first dashed curve appear only on `0 < η <= 1` and the second only on `-1 < η <= 0`.

If you want a more general solution, `RegionFunction` also works:

```wl

 RegionFunction -> Function[{x, y}, y1[x] < y2[x]]
]
```

Or in shorthand form:

```wl

```

but for multiple curves with different cutoffs, `ConditionalExpression` is usually more direct.

`Exclusions` does not usually stop `Plot3D` from *sampling* points near the singularity. It mainly tells the plotting routine not to draw the surface across the excluded set. So if the function evaluates at `x == y` during adaptive sampling, you can still get “intermediate value” messages.

A few practical fixes:

1. Suppress the messages
```wl
Plot3D[Quiet@f[x, y, 5, -1, 3], {x, 9, 10}, {y, 9, 10},
 Exclusions -> x == y]
```

2. Define the function so it is undefined on the singular set
```wl
f1[x_, y_, a_, b_, c_] := ((E^(b x) - E^(b y)) x)/((c E^(a b) + E^(b x)) (x - y)) /; x != y
```

or explicitly return `Indeterminate`:
```wl
f2[x_, y_, a_, b_, c_] := If[x == y,
  Indeterminate,
  ((E^(b x) - E^(b y)) x)/((c E^(a b) + E^(b x)) (x - y))
]
```

Then plot:
```wl
Plot3D[f2[x, y, 5, -1, 3], {x, 9, 10}, {y, 9, 10},
 Exclusions -> x == y]
```

If you want to exclude a band like `-0.1 <= x - y <= 0.1`, use:
```wl
Exclusions -> Abs[x - y] <= 0.1
```

or equivalently:
```wl
Exclusions -> -0.1 <= x - y <= 0.1
```

But note: this still won’t necessarily prevent evaluation there unless the function itself handles those points cleanly. The most robust approach is to make the function return `Indeterminate` or use a condition in the definition.

In Mathematica/Wolfram Language, pattern specificity is decided by the pattern matcher using a hierarchy of how constrained the pattern is.

General idea:
- More explicit patterns are considered more specific.
- Exact values are more specific than types.
- Typed patterns are more specific than wildcards.
- Patterns with conditions or structural restrictions are more specific than unconstrained patterns.

For example:
- `x_` is less specific than `x_Integer`
- `x_Integer` is less specific than `x_Integer?Positive`
- `{a_, b_}` is more specific than `_List`
- `f[1, y_]` is more specific than `f[x_, y_]`

If multiple definitions could match, Mathematica chooses the one it judges most specific. If it still can’t decide, you may get an ambiguity warning.

A practical way to think about it:
- Literal elements win over patterns.
- Narrower domains win over broader ones.
- Additional structure makes a pattern more specific.

Pattern specificity in Mathematica is determined by the actual pattern structure, not by what the pattern evaluates to or what it may “look like” after substitution.

In your case, the key point is:

- `_Integer` does not match the special rule’s left-hand pattern
- because that special rule expects something of the form `x[]` in the second argument
- while `_` is just a blank pattern, not an expression of the form `x[]`

So Mathematica falls back to the catch-all rule.

Also, your `MatchQ[...]` test is misleading because the arguments are evaluated first. So:

- `PatternImplies[_Integer, _]` evaluates to `Maybe`
- then you are effectively testing `MatchQ[Maybe, Maybe]`, which is `True`

If you want to test the pattern structure itself, use `Hold`:

```wl
MatchQ[
  Hold@PatternImplies[_Integer, _],
  Hold@PatternImplies[(x:(Verbatim[Blank] | Verbatim[BlankSequence] | Verbatim[BlankNullSequence]))[h_], x[]]
]
```

This returns `False`.

One more important correction: if you meant “a pattern with the same head as `x`”, you likely want `x_[]`, not `x[]`.

- `x[]` means literally the expression `x` with no arguments
- `x_[]` means “any zero-argument expression whose head matches the previous pattern `x`”

So the rule should probably be written with `x_[]` if that was your intention.

Pattern specificity is mainly decided by the pattern matcher’s ability to rule out candidates early and to avoid repeated evaluation/copying during matching.

A few practical rules:

1. More structural information = more specific
- `f[{a_, b_}]` is more specific than `f[{x__}]`
- `f[x_Integer]` is more specific than `f[x_]`
- `f[x_String]` is more specific than `f[x_?StringQ]` in performance terms, because the latter may invoke the evaluator repeatedly

2. “Syntactic” patterns are those that avoid evaluator calls
- Typically: blanks (`_`), typed blanks (`_Integer`, `_String`, etc.), sequences (`__`, `___`), and structural forms made from these
- Slower forms usually involve:
  - `Condition` (`/;`)
  - `PatternTest` (`?`)
  - anything that forces the evaluator to run during matching

So the earlier remark is not just about `Cases`; it’s a general pattern-matching performance issue. The exact impact varies by construct, but the same underlying costs apply in `MatchQ`, `ReplaceAll`, `Cases`, `ReplaceRepeated`, function definitions, etc.

3. Avoid patterns that generate many failed attempts
- `___` and `__` are powerful but can cause many backtracking attempts
- This is especially costly in repeated rewriting (`//.`) or when many positions are tried
- Example: rules like `{left___, x_, y_, right___}` can be expensive because the matcher explores many splits

4. Avoid patterns that force large copies
- Sequence patterns can copy large parts of expressions, especially lists
- That may be acceptable for small expressions, but expensive for large arrays/lists

5. If you need a test, prefer structural restrictions first, then a test if needed
- Better: `x_Integer /; x > 0`
- But if possible, narrow the structure before testing so fewer candidates reach the test

6. Optimization is worth it when matching is done often
- For one-off matches, readability usually matters more
- For tight loops, large data, or repeated rewriting, pattern design can matter a lot

In short:

- “Syntactic pattern” usually means a pattern that relies on structure/type rather than evaluator-based tests.
- That style is generally faster across pattern-matching constructs, not only `Cases`.
- `BlankNullSequence` and similar constructs are not inherently bad, but they can become expensive when they create lots of backtracking or copying.
- If performance matters, first make the pattern more structurally specific; only then add semantic tests if necessary.

If your goal is to return Mathematica to a “fresh” state after startup packages have been loaded, the usual options are:

1. Use CleanSlate`
- This is the closest thing to “unload everything I loaded and go back to defaults.”
- You can call it later in the session when you want to clear user-defined symbols and contexts.
- It may help even if your startup package modified some symbols, but anything that has been deeply altered in System` can be harder to fully restore, depending on what was changed.

2. Unload only specific packages
- If you only want to remove certain packages, use PackageManipulations` and its PackageRemove function.
- That package also includes:
  - PackageClear
  - PackageClearComplete
- These are useful if you want to clear package symbols without fully removing the package context.

Important caution:
- Removing package symbols can break other packages if they depend on them.
- If other packages reference symbols from the package you remove, those references can become Removed[symbol], which can cause subtle failures.
- To check dependencies, the same author provides PackageSymbolsDependencies`.

For your specific setup:
- Yes, you can include CleanSlate` in init.m and use it later when you want to revert.
- But it is usually not something you would use automatically every time Mathematica starts, unless you really want a very clean environment.
- If your startup package modifies System` symbols, test carefully: CleanSlate` is helpful, but it may not undo every kind of modification in a perfectly safe way.

- Stronger editing support: autocomplete, inspections, syntax highlighting, bracket matching
- Project structure: easier to manage larger codebases with many `.m`/`.wl` files
- Version control integration: Git, diff/merge, history
- Testing/build workflows: more convenient for package development and automated scripts
- Team collaboration: easier for multiple developers to work on shared code

Where it helps less:
- Exploratory computation and ad hoc analysis
- Notebook-centric workflows
- Visual/interactive work that is naturally done in the Wolfram Notebook interface

So for a scientist mostly doing calculations, modeling, and notebook-based exploration, IntelliJ IDEA is usually not essential. It becomes more valuable when your Mathematica work turns into a larger maintainable codebase, package development, or collaborative software project.

If you want, I can also compare IntelliJ IDEA vs the Wolfram front end for specific tasks like package development, debugging, or large project organization.

Yes — but not directly in the sense of “the kernel automatically compiles an arbitrary user-defined `NormFunction` and uses it as the default.” In `NDSolve`, a user-supplied `NormFunction` is typically called from the Wolfram Language side unless you provide something the solver can use efficiently.

A good approach is to define the norm as a compiled function yourself and then pass that function to `NormFunction`.

Example:

```wl
cf = Compile[{{x, _Real, 1}},
  Max[Abs[Take[x, 2]]],
  CompilationTarget -> "C",
  RuntimeOptions -> "Speed"
];
```

Then use:

```wl
NDSolve[
  {...},
  y,
  {t, t0, t1},
  NormFunction -> (cf[#] &)
]
```

A few notes:

- `NormFunction` is expected to take the state vector as its argument.
- For best performance, keep the function simple and numeric.
- `Compile` helps most when the function is called many times during integration.
- If you use constructs like `Take` inside a compiled function, make sure the argument type is a packed numeric vector (`_Real, 1`), as above.

If you want the exact infinity norm on the first two components, `Max[Abs[Take[x, 2]]]` is a direct compiled equivalent of:

```wl
Norm[Take[#, 2], Infinity] &
```

If you find that `Compile` still doesn’t speed things up enough, another option is to define the norm inline in a way the solver can optimize better, but in general the compiled function is the right answer here.

If you want, I can also show a version that avoids `Take` and is a bit more compilation-friendly.

Use a delayed rule, `:>`, instead of an immediate rule, `->`.

With `->`, the right-hand side is evaluated before the pattern variables are substituted, so `amp` and `afreq` remain as symbols in the resulting function.

Try:

```wl
s = {10 Cos[-Pi t], -4 Sin[0.23 t]};

f2[a1_, a2_, a3_] := Module[
  {a = a1, phi = a3},
  Function[a a2[phi #1]]
];

f1 := Function[f2[#1, #2, #3]];

l = Cases[s, amp_ trig_[afreq_ t] :> f1[amp, trig, afreq]];
l[[1]][.33]
```

This gives a numeric result, e.g.

```wl
5.09041
```

Why:

- `->` evaluates the replacement expression first.
- `:>` waits until a match is found, then substitutes the matched values into the right-hand side.

So for pattern-based function construction, `:>` is usually the right choice.

There isn’t a built-in `MaxProcessorUsed` / `MaxCPUUsed` analog in Mathematica/Wolfram Language comparable to `MaxMemoryUsed`.

A few practical options:

1. Time the code
- `Timing[...]` or `AbsoluteTiming[...]` are the standard tools.
- For nested functions, wrap the whole outer call, or instrument inner calls separately.

2. Measure CPU time, not just wall time
- `TimeConstrained` limits wall-clock time, but doesn’t measure usage.
- Use `TimeUsed[]` before and after a computation to get CPU time consumed by the current kernel.
- Example:
  ```wl
  t0 = TimeUsed[];
  expr;
  t1 = TimeUsed[];
  t1 - t0
  ```

3. Profile where time goes
- `Trace` can help, but for performance analysis `WolframSystem` profiling tools are more useful:
  - `RepeatedTiming`
  - `Developer` context functions in some versions
  - `$HistoryLength = 0` can reduce notebook overhead during tests

4. If you want “current CPU load”
- Wolfram Language does not provide a portable built-in for live process CPU utilization like an OS task manager.
- You’d typically need external OS commands via `RunProcess`, `Import`, or platform-specific tools.

5. For GUI/Dynamic responsiveness
- Measure the code executed by `Dynamic` separately.
- Keep `Dynamic` bodies small and use `TrackedSymbols`, `SynchronousUpdating -> False`, `UpdateInterval`, etc.
- Often the right question is not “CPU %” but “how long does this update take?” because UI lag is mainly perceived latency.

For nested functions specifically, if you want precise timing of each layer, the usual approach is manual instrumentation:

```wl
ClearAll[withTiming];
withTiming[label_, expr_] := Module[{t, res},
  t = AbsoluteTiming[res = expr;][[1]];
  Print[label, ": ", t, " s"];
  res
]
```

Then:
```wl
outer[] := withTiming["outer", inner1[] + inner2[]]
```

If you want, I can show you a small reusable timing/profiling wrapper for nested Wolfram Language functions that records inclusive vs. exclusive time.

The main issue here is not `Timing` itself, but what your expression is actually doing.

With

```wl
M = Partition[Range@10000000, 1000];
V = Range[10000] - 1;
```

`M` is a packed array, but `V` has the wrong length for a row of `M`. So

```wl
Prepend[M, V]
```

forces unpacking of the array, and that unpacking dominates the runtime. That is why the timings look unexpectedly large and somewhat inconsistent.

If you use a vector of matching length, the behavior changes completely:

```wl
V = Range[1000] - 1;
Table[Prepend[M, V]; // Timing // First, {10}]
```

you get timings near zero or near the clock resolution, because no unpacking is needed.

Also, if you explicitly unpack just the top level:

```wl
M = List @@ Partition[Range@10000000, 1000];
V = Range[10000] - 1;
Table[Prepend[M, V]; // Timing // First, {10}]
```

then the operation is essentially instantaneous, because the expensive packed-array behavior is gone.

So the “jump” in timing is mostly about unpacking, not about `Timing` becoming unreliable for the first measurement.

As for `timeAvg`: it can be useful as a workaround when you want to average over several repeated evaluations and reduce clock-resolution noise, especially for very fast expressions. But it is not a substitute for understanding what is being measured. For heavier expressions like this, it may hide the real issue.

In short:

- `Timing` is not the main problem here.
- Your expression triggers unpacking.
- Use matching dimensions if you want a fair benchmark.
- Use `timeAvg` only when you need better resolution for very fast code, not as a general fix.

Yes — the usual easy way is to add custom `Epilog` graphics at parameter values of interest.

For a parametric curve `f[t] = {x[t], y[t]}`, you can:

1. pick the parameter values where you want ticks,
2. compute the point on the curve,
3. compute a short line segment perpendicular to the curve there,
4. add a label with `Text`.

A compact pattern is:

```wl
inward[f_, t_] := RotationTransform[Pi/2][Normalize[f'[t]]]

tickGraphics[f_] := Function[{t, text},
  {
    Line[{f[t], f[t] + 0.02 inward[f, t]}],
    Text[text, f[t] + 0.05 inward[f, t]]
  }
]
```

Then use it in `ParametricPlot`:

```wl
ParametricPlot[fun[d], {d, -2000, 2000},
  FrameLabel -> {"A_{22}", "A_{44}"},
  PlotRange -> {{-0.4, 0.5}, {-0.1, 0.4}},
  PlotPoints -> 1000,
  Epilog -> (tickGraphics[fun] @@@
    ({d, t} /. Flatten[
      Solve[{d/(1 + Abs[d]) == #, t == #}, {d, t}] & /@ Range[-0.8, 0.8, 0.2],
      1
    ]))
]
```

That approach labels the curve with values of the transformed parameter `d/(1+Abs[d])`.

If you want a simpler demo version, this works too:

```wl
f[t_] := Evaluate[((2 Pi + t)/(4 Pi)) RotationTransform[Pi/4][{1, 2} RotationTransform[t][{1, 0}]]]

inward[f_, t_] := RotationTransform[Pi/2][Normalize[f'[t]]]

tickGraphics[f_] := Function[t,
  {Line[{f[t], f[t] + inward[f, t]/10}],
   Text[t, f[t] + inward[f, t]/5]}
]

ParametricPlot[f[t], {t, 0, 2 Pi},
  Epilog -> (tickGraphics[f] /@ Range[0, 2 Pi, Pi/6]),
  AspectRatio -> Automatic,
  Axes -> False
]
```

So in short: yes, the “easy way” is custom ticks made with `Epilog`, `Line`, and `Text`. If you want, I can also show how to make the tick labels appear on the frame instead of on the curve itself.

For `Histogram`, `AbsoluteOptions[..., PlotRange]` can fail because the object may internally store a symbolic PlotRange specification like `{{All,All},{-4.,0.}}`, which is not a fully numeric range.

A simple way to get the actual y-range from the histogram is:

```wl
data = {-1.2056, -1.46192, -1.30053, -2.52879, -0.99636, -1.73904, -1.164,
   -1.83398, -0.97505, -0.503256, -0.63802, -0.785963, -0.711821,
   -0.820439, -1.8699, -3.9659, -1.4456, -1.67021, -1.42009, -2.5644,
   -1.45002, -1.27806, -1.66529, -1.67073, -3.31102, -3.38638};

hist = Histogram[data, PlotRange -> Automatic];

First[PlotRange /. Options[hist, PlotRange]]
```

This gives the stored `PlotRange` specification.

If you want the actual numeric vertical range, use:

```wl
AbsoluteOptions[hist, PlotRange] /. PlotRange -> pr_ :> pr
```

But for `Histogram`, the most direct reliable approach is often to inspect the option directly as above.

If you specifically want the y-axis range, you can extract it from the returned option:

```wl
(PlotRange /. Options[hist, PlotRange])[[2]]
```

In your example, that corresponds to the vertical range.

In older versions of Mathematica/Wolfram Language, `AbsoluteOptions[..., PlotRange]` could be unreliable when `PlotRange` was implicit (`Automatic`, `All`, etc.). So for a histogram or other graphics, it might not report the actual rendered range.

If you need the real plot range, a common workaround is to infer it from generated ticks after forcing the graphics to render.

For example:

```wl
completePlotRange[plot : (_Graphics | _Graphics3D | _Graph)] :=
  Last @ Last @ Reap[
    Rasterize[
      Show[plot,
        Axes -> True,
        Frame -> False,
        Ticks -> ((Sow[{##}]; Automatic) &),
        DisplayFunction -> Identity,
        ImageSize -> 0
      ],
      ImageResolution -> 1
    ]
  ]
```

If you want the exact range without `PlotRangePadding`, use:

```wl
plotRange[plot : (_Graphics | _Graphics3D | _Graph)] :=
  Last @ Last @ Reap[
    Rasterize[
      Show[plot,
        PlotRangePadding -> None,
        Axes -> True,
        Frame -> False,
        Ticks -> ((Sow[{##}]; Automatic) &),
        DisplayFunction -> Identity,
        ImageSize -> 0
      ],
      ImageResolution -> 1
    ]
  ]
```

Example use:

```wl
plotRange[Histogram[RandomVariate[NormalDistribution[], 100]]]
```

Note: in Wolfram Language 13.0.0 and later, this specific `AbsoluteOptions` PlotRange bug was reported as fixed. So if you are on a recent version, `AbsoluteOptions` may now behave correctly.

The main difference is:

- `Set` (`=`) evaluates the right-hand side immediately and stores the result.
- `SetDelayed` (`:=`) stores the expression unevaluated and re-evaluates it each time the left-hand side is used.

So these can behave the same in simple cases, but not always.

A concrete difference after definition is done:

```wl
x = {1, 2, 3};
x[[2]] = 8
```

works, because `x` already has an immediate value.

But:

```wl
y := {1, 2, 3};
y[[2]] = 8
```

fails with:

```wl
Set::noval: Symbol y in part assignment does not have an immediate value
```

So Mathematica does keep track of whether the definition was immediate or delayed, and that can affect later behavior.

In short:

- `=`: compute now, store value now
- `:=`: store rule, compute later when needed

Even if `OwnValues` / `DownValues` look similar, the system still distinguishes them internally.
